```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-studio-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Produce:</b> a design card for one brief: its scale, its <span class="lx-term" data-term="system-boundary">boundary</span> (decided or computed, fixed inputs, left out), a time step and horizon, a method family, and a defence of that method against two alternatives.</li>
<li><b>From:</b> three illustrative briefs at three scales, each a different type of question.</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> the card states the scale, the three boundary lists, a time step and horizon, and a method defended against two alternatives, one from another family; your R1 card covers the rest of Framing.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 30 minutes guided here, then about an hour on your own: take your own question card from <a href="r01-framing.html">R1</a> through the same moves, and write the defence in the same six parts.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="r03-system-and-method" data-src="../assets/learn/data/r03-system-and-method.json ../assets/learn/data/path.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The moves, in order</p>
<ol>
<li>Place the question on the scale ladder: device and plant, microgrid and community, regional grid, city and region, nation.</li>
<li>Draw its boundary: what the study decides or computes, the fixed inputs it uses but does not change, and what it leaves out and says so.</li>
<li>Pick a time step that shows what the metric needs, and a horizon that covers the decision.</li>
<li>Choose a method family, then defend it against a simpler version and against another family, and name its main limit.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Three briefs, with a researcher's answers</p>
<!-- r03-task:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Keep the hospital running (prescriptive, S1)</summary>
<p><strong>What sizes of solar, battery and backup generator keep Prairie Campus's hospital supplied through a three-day winter outage at the lowest 20-year cost, compared with today's diesel generator alone?</strong></p>
<p class="lx-hint">Assumed: the switch to running alone (<span class="lx-term" data-term="islanding">islanding</span>) works. The study checks whether there is enough energy, not the switch itself.</p>
<ul><li><strong>Scale:</strong> S1: one campus that can run on its own, sized by its owner under the utility's rules. The tariff and the feeder's limits come from the regional grid above.</li>
<li><strong>Decided or computed</strong> (in the study: it decides or computes these):<ul><li>Sizes of solar, battery and generator (These are the decisions the study makes)</li></ul></li>
<li><strong>Fixed inputs</strong> (in the study: used, but not changed by it):<ul><li>The hospital's critical load, hour by hour (A measured or estimated input; the study does not change it)</li><li>The utility's tariff and the feeder's export limit (Set at the scale above; fixed inputs here)</li><li>Hourly winter weather for solar output (An input: a design winter, or several past ones)</li><li>Diesel fuel stored on site when the outage starts (A fixed limit in the outage case)</li></ul></li>
<li><strong>Left out</strong> (outside the study: stated as a limit):<ul><li>Wholesale prices across the Plains Grid (The campus pays a tariff, not wholesale prices: say so as a limit)</li><li>Road access for fuel trucks during the storm (Left out and stated: the design must last three days on stored fuel)</li><li>Who owns the system and who pays for it (A separate question about ownership, noted as a limit of the cost result)</li></ul></li>
<li><strong>Time step and horizon:</strong> 1 hour, hourly steps follow solar's daily cycle and the battery's charge; a typical year plus the outage.</li>
<li><strong>Fits well:</strong> Optimization, Simulation, Mixed methods.</li>
<li><strong>Helps with a part:</strong> Statistics and econometrics, Qualitative methods.</li>
<li><strong>Poor fit for this question:</strong> Machine learning, System dynamics, Agent-based modelling, Equilibrium modelling.</li>
<li><strong>A researcher's defence (Optimization):</strong><ul><li><b>Family:</b> Optimization</li><li><b>Method:</b> A sizing <span class="lx-term" data-term="mixed-integer-program">mixed-integer program</span> (MILP) that picks the cheapest sizes keeping the critical load served.</li><li><b>Time step and horizon:</b> Hourly steps over a typical year, plus a three-day winter outage.</li><li><b>Alternative 1:</b> a <span class="lx-term" data-term="linear-program">linear program</span> (LP) with continuous sizes</li><li><b>Why not alternative 1:</b> The generator has a minimum load and comes in whole units, which only whole-number decisions capture.</li><li><b>Alternative 2:</b> Simulation</li><li><b>Why not alternative 2:</b> The question asks for the cheapest mix, not a ranking of mixes I already have; a simulation still checks the chosen design.</li><li><b>Main limit:</b> <span class="lx-term" data-term="perfect-foresight">Perfect foresight</span> during the outage: the model knows the coming weather.</li><li><b>Reduced or checked by:</b> Test the chosen design in a rule-based simulation that does not know the future.</li></ul></li></ul></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Did the rebate reach low-income homes? (evaluative, S3)</summary>
<p><strong>Did Prairie City's 2023 heat-pump rebate raise installations in its low-income neighbourhoods, compared with similar neighbourhoods in cities without a rebate?</strong></p>
<ul><li><strong>Scale:</strong> S3: a city programme, set by the council with local money and rules. Federal incentives come from the nation above; the homes below act on them.</li>
<li><strong>Decided or computed</strong> (in the study: it decides or computes these):<ul><li>Heat-pump installations per 1,000 homes, by neighbourhood and month (The outcome the study measures)</li><li>The choice of comparison neighbourhoods (A design decision of the study, and the one that matters most)</li></ul></li>
<li><strong>Fixed inputs</strong> (in the study: used, but not changed by it):<ul><li>The rebate's rules, amount and start date (Fixed facts of the programme)</li><li>Neighbourhood income and housing data from the census (Input data, used to match similar neighbourhoods)</li><li>Federal tax credits available everywhere (Assumed to affect both groups alike; check eligibility and other policies that could shift their trends differently)</li></ul></li>
<li><strong>Left out</strong> (outside the study: stated as a limit):<ul><li>Whether the heat pumps lowered bills (A different question, for a later study)</li><li>Installers' waiting lists (Left out and stated: they may have limited uptake)</li><li>Grid upgrades for the new heating load (Outside a question about uptake)</li></ul></li>
<li><strong>Time step and horizon:</strong> 1 month, monthly counts show the change around the rebate's start; 2019 to 2025, before and after.</li>
<li><strong>Fits well:</strong> Statistics and econometrics, Mixed methods.</li>
<li><strong>Helps with a part:</strong> Machine learning, Agent-based modelling, Qualitative methods.</li>
<li><strong>Poor fit for this question:</strong> Optimization, Simulation, System dynamics, Equilibrium modelling.</li>
<li><strong>A researcher's defence (Statistics and econometrics):</strong><ul><li><b>Family:</b> Statistics and econometrics</li><li><b>Method:</b> A <span class="lx-term" data-term="difference-in-differences">difference-in-differences</span> comparison of installations in low-income neighbourhoods.</li><li><b>Time step and horizon:</b> Monthly installations by neighbourhood, 2019 to 2025.</li><li><b>Alternative 1:</b> a before-and-after count in Prairie City alone</li><li><b>Why not alternative 1:</b> Prices and federal credits changed everywhere at once, so a before-and-after count mixes them with the rebate.</li><li><b>Alternative 2:</b> Agent-based modelling</li><li><b>Why not alternative 2:</b> It would assume how households respond, which is what this study must measure.</li><li><b>Main limit:</b> It assumes both groups would have moved in parallel without the rebate.</li><li><b>Reduced or checked by:</b> Compare their trends before 2023, and repeat with a second comparison group.</li></ul></li></ul></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>A large load that can pause (predictive, S2)</summary>
<p><strong>How would a 300 MW load that can pause for up to four hours during scarcity change the Plains Grid's <span class="lx-term" data-term="expected-unserved-energy">expected unserved energy</span> in a heat-wave year, compared with the same load running flat?</strong></p>
<p class="lx-hint">Pausing rule (illustrative): up to four hours in a row per event, at most ten events a year, and paused work is not made up later. Paused energy is counted apart from unserved energy.</p>
<ul><li><strong>Scale:</strong> S2: <span class="lx-term" data-term="resource-adequacy">adequacy</span> is planned for a region, such as a market operator's or a utility's planning area, with its transfer limits and assumptions about its neighbours. The load only decides when it pauses.</li>
<li><strong>Decided or computed</strong> (in the study: it decides or computes these):<ul><li>When the load pauses, hour by hour (Set inside the study by a pausing rule)</li><li>Random generator outages (Drawn many times by the study, to give a range)</li></ul></li>
<li><strong>Fixed inputs</strong> (in the study: used, but not changed by it):<ul><li>Hourly demand and weather for a heat-wave year (Input data: a past heat-wave year, or a scaled one)</li><li>Today's plants and the transfer limits between zones (Fixed: the question asks about the system as it is)</li><li>Imports from neighbouring grids (Fixed limits, stated)</li></ul></li>
<li><strong>Left out</strong> (outside the study: stated as a limit):<ul><li>The load's contract: who pays for pausing (A separate question about contracts and tariffs)</li><li>Voltage and stability in the seconds after a trip (A different time scale, and a different study)</li><li>New plants built because the load arrived (A planning question; this one keeps the fleet fixed)</li></ul></li>
<li><strong>Time step and horizon:</strong> 1 hour, adequacy studies count unserved energy hour by hour; one year, run many times.</li>
<li><strong>Fits well:</strong> Simulation.</li>
<li><strong>Helps with a part:</strong> Optimization, Statistics and econometrics, Agent-based modelling, Qualitative methods, Mixed methods.</li>
<li><strong>Poor fit for this question:</strong> Machine learning, System dynamics, Equilibrium modelling.</li>
<li><strong>A researcher's defence (Simulation):</strong><ul><li><b>Family:</b> Simulation</li><li><b>Method:</b> A <span class="lx-term" data-term="monte-carlo">Monte Carlo</span> adequacy simulation that runs the heat-wave year many times with random outages.</li><li><b>Time step and horizon:</b> Hourly steps; one year, run many times.</li><li><b>Alternative 1:</b> a check of the single worst hour</li><li><b>Why not alternative 1:</b> The question asks how often and how much, not only whether.</li><li><b>Alternative 2:</b> Optimization</li><li><b>Why not alternative 2:</b> The question keeps today's plants and asks for a risk, not a plan.</li><li><b>Main limit:</b> Outages are drawn independently, while a heat wave can cause several at once.</li><li><b>Reduced or checked by:</b> Add a run with linked outages as a sensitivity.</li></ul></li></ul></details>
<!-- r03-task:end -->
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you make each choice yourself, with a note on how well it fits, and your design stays in this browser.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><span>The briefs, Prairie Campus, Prairie City, the Plains Grid and the 300 MW load are illustrative. The fit notes are teaching judgements, not rules: several method families can answer one question well.</span></p>
```

## Two answers to the same task
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r03-exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<p>Defend a method for: “How sensitive is a national storage build-out to a one-year disruption of one mineral, and which design choices reduce the risk?”</p>
<!-- r03-exemplars:start (written from the data file by LX.Exemplars' staticHTML, and the method families from the data file, in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak answer · Developing</p><p class="lx-ex-lines">Method: capacity-expansion optimization [1]
Why: it is the standard tool for national planning [2]
Result: it gives the optimal answer [3]
Covers: the whole country [4]</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> A family is named, but nothing says why it fits a question about sensitivity and risk.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> Chosen by habit: the rubric's Developing anchor for method fit.</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> Optimal only inside the model's assumptions, and one run gives no range.</li><li value="4"><b>Falls short:</b> A scale, but no boundary, time step or horizon.</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong answer · Strong on method fit</p><p class="lx-ex-lines">Reading: a conditional planning study: how do model-optimal storage plans change across disruption cases? [1]
Scale and boundary: S4; the national power system's builds and hourly operation; mineral supply enters as given disruption cases; recycling left out [2]
Method: a capacity-expansion model (optimization), run under many disruption cases drawn at random [3]
Time step and horizon: yearly steps to 2040, representative hours inside each year [4]
Alternative 1: a single run with expected prices [5]; it hides the risk the question asks about
Alternative 2: a system-dynamics model of mineral supply [6]; it captures market feedback, not the grid's hourly needs
Main limit: perfect foresight inside each case; the results are model-optimal plans, not predicted deployment [7]
Reduced by: fixing early builds before the disruption is known [8]</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> Says what an optimization can answer here: the best plan under each case, not a forecast of what will be built.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> The three boundary lists: what is decided or computed, what is fixed and what is left out.</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> Matches the question: “how sensitive” needs a range, not one plan.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> Time step and horizon stated, matched to a build-out over years.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> A simpler version of the same family, rejected for a reason.</li><li value="6"><b>Works:</b> Another family, rejected for a reason: what the Proficient anchor asks for.</li><li value="7"><b>Works:</b> The limit stated, with what the results do and do not mean.</li><li value="8"><b>Works:</b> The limit partly mitigated: the Strong anchor for method fit.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<table class="lx-facts lx-ex-diff"><thead><tr><th scope="col"></th><th scope="col">Weak answer</th><th scope="col">Strong answer</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Why this family</th><td>Habit</td><td>Tied to what the question asks</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Boundary</th><td>“The whole country”</td><td>Decided, fixed and left out</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Time step and horizon</th><td>Not stated</td><td>Yearly to 2040, representative hours</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Alternatives</th><td>None</td><td>One in the family, one from another</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Limit</th><td>None</td><td>Stated, what results mean, partly reduced</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Nine method families, side by side</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Family</th><th scope="col">Answers</th><th scope="col">Needs</th><th scope="col">Main limit</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Optimization</td><td>What is the best choice under stated rules and goals?</td><td>Decisions, a goal, rules (constraints) and their data.</td><td>Best only inside the model, for its stated goal; a full-horizon run also assumes <span class="lx-term" data-term="perfect-foresight">perfect foresight</span>, unless built to decide step by step (a rolling horizon).</td></tr><tr><td>Simulation</td><td>What happens when the system runs by given rules, under given conditions?</td><td>Operating rules, inputs over time and the designs to test.</td><td>It tests the designs you give it; it does not search for the best one.</td></tr><tr><td>Statistics and econometrics</td><td>How much, how often, and did a change cause an effect?</td><td>Observed data with variation; for a causal claim, a comparison group.</td><td>It sees only the observed past; causal claims rest on assumptions about the comparison.</td></tr><tr><td>Machine learning</td><td>What will the next value be, or which pattern is this?</td><td>Many examples, honest baselines and data held back for testing.</td><td>Least reliable outside the range of its training data, and it explains little about why.</td></tr><tr><td>System dynamics</td><td>How do stocks, flows and feedback shape a trend over years?</td><td>A causal-loop structure and parameters for each flow.</td><td>It works with aggregates, and many parameters rest on judgement.</td></tr><tr><td>Agent-based modelling</td><td>How do many deciding actors produce a system outcome?</td><td>Rules for each kind of actor, and data on how they behave.</td><td>Results depend on behaviour rules that are hard to check against data.</td></tr><tr><td>Equilibrium modelling</td><td>Where do prices and quantities settle when many markets or players interact?</td><td>Supply and demand, market rules and how players respond to prices.</td><td>Static versions describe a settled state, not the path to it; most simplify how players behave.</td></tr><tr><td>Qualitative methods</td><td>How and why do people and institutions decide as they do?</td><td>Interviews, documents or cases, with consent and a plan for the analysis.</td><td>It gives no numbers that generalise; this course teaches it at awareness level only.</td></tr><tr><td>Mixed methods</td><td>Questions that need both numbers and people's reasons.</td><td>A model or data analysis, a qualitative part, and a plan for how each informs the other.</td><td>More time, and both parts must answer the same question.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<!-- r03-exemplars:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

## Check your own work against the rubric
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r03-rubric" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r03-rubric:start (written by LX.Rubric's staticHTML, from the course rubric, and the scales from the data file, in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts lx-rb-static"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Competence</th><th scope="col">Developing</th><th scope="col">Proficient (the bar)</th><th scope="col">Strong</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Framing<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: the scale and the three boundary lists are stated; the rest of Framing (audience, metric with units, counterfactual, falsification) comes from your R1 card.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Question vague or untyped; no audience or counterfactual.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Typed question with audience or decision-maker, metric with units, counterfactual, scale and boundary; one falsification statement.</td><td data-l="Strong">Also explains why the question matters to its audience and what answer would change a decision.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Method fit<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: two alternatives named, one from another family, each rejected for a reason tied to the question.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Method chosen by habit.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Method defended against two alternatives, one of them a different family.</td><td data-l="Strong">Limits of the chosen method stated and partly mitigated.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Five scales: who decides, and typical steps and horizons</p>
<ul><li><b>S0 Device and plant:</b> decides what to install at one site, and how to run it; the owner, within tariffs and codes. Time step: minutes to an hour; horizon: a day to the equipment's life.</li><li><b>S1 Microgrid and community:</b> decides sizes, islanding, load priorities, ownership; a facility owner or co-op, under the utility's rules. Time step: minutes to an hour; horizon: an outage to about 20 years.</li><li><b>S2 Regional grid:</b> decides commitment, dispatch, reserves, transmission, new plants; the grid operator or utility, and regulators. Time step: seconds to an hour; horizon: the next hour to several decades.</li><li><b>S3 City and region:</b> decides buildings, heat, transport, land use, local supply; city and county, utilities and owners. Time step: an hour to a year; horizon: to 2040 or 2050.</li><li><b>S4 Nation:</b> decides targets, policy instruments, infrastructure, security stocks, trade; national governments and regulators. Time step: representative hours to a year; horizon: decades.</li></ul>
<!-- r03-rubric:end -->
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="r3-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="detail" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A more detailed model is always more accurate.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Detail adds data needs and uncertainty of its own; match the detail to the question, and say what you left out.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="optimal" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An optimal plan predicts what will happen.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It is the best plan under the model's assumptions; real decisions and real paths depart from it, which is why a prescriptive answer comes with its limits.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="leftout" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Saying what a study leaves out makes its answer more useful, not less.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. A reader can only use an answer if they know where it holds; an unstated <span class="lx-term" data-term="system-boundary">boundary</span> invites them to use it where it does not.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>Where the defence goes next</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>In the research capstone (CR, upcoming), this design card becomes the method section of your proposal; the mock review in CK-R asks you to defend it again.</p>
<p>The Modeler lessons build the families in depth:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html">M1</a>: a dispatch linear program.</li>
<li><a href="m02-unit-commitment.html">M2</a>: unit commitment.</li>
<li><a href="m03-capacity-expansion.html">M3</a>: capacity expansion.</li>
<li>Uncertainty and data analysis: in the lessons to come.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this studio leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Spatial resolution: zones, buses, neighbourhoods or grid cells matter as much as the time step, and are chosen the same way.</li>
<li>Coupling models: many studies link two families, for example an optimization inside a Monte Carlo loop. The “mixed” label here covers only models with a qualitative part.</li>
<li>Qualitative methods are taught at awareness level only; a fully qualitative study needs a mentor trained in them.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
